q: Who should lead off for the A's next season, and why?
text:
Here's my answer, Anthony, on the record:

**Danny Horn leads off. It isn't close.**

The case is simple and it's in my records. Horn is the only hitter on this roster who does both leadoff jobs at an elite level: he gets on and he runs. Last season, 2041, he hit .338 with a .382 on-base, and he stole 80 bases in 148 games. Nobody else on the club is within reach of that combination — Darrin Davis stole 26 with a .350 OBP, Taveras has 2 steals and a .339 OBP, Gonzalez stole 17 at .349. Horn is the only one who turns a single into a run-scoring situation at a rate that matters.

And his ratings moved the right way this winter: contact vs RHP +10 to 95, vs LHP +3 to 80, vision +9 to 87, power vs RHP +7 to 85. He's a switch-hitter, so there's no platoon hole at the top, and his 92 speed and 83 stealing are still there at 31. He also only struck out 65 times last year against 35 walks — for a man with 56 home runs, that's an unusually clean at-bat.

The one thing I'll flag honestly: his discipline rating dropped 12 points, to 66, and he's a Day Player whose performance dips in night games. If you wanted a purist's on-base man, the argument would be Vladimir Gonzalez — 95 vision, 80 discipline, .349 OBP — but Gonzalez has a 60 speed and 66 stealing, and you don't put a 99 clutch, pull-hitting run producer at the top of the order to have him standing on first when the middle of the order comes up.

My working lineup top would be Horn in center and leading off, Gonzalez second or third, and the RBI bats behind them. But the leadoff answer is Horn, and I'd be surprised if it changes by Opening Day.

One caveat as always: everything I just gave you comes from my records and my ratings sheets. If the Tribune wants a current medical or a fresh report from the coaching staff, that's not a thing my records hold, and I won't pretend otherwise.

q: How does the A's rotation line up for 2042, one through five?
text:
Here's how I'd line it up, Anthony — one through five:

1. **Travis Coles** — 22, overall 99, the reigning Cy Young winner. 22–4, 2.72, 254 strikeouts in 215.1 innings, 6.2 WAR, and he goes five pitches deep with a 98 mph fastball. He's the ace, and I don't think that's a close call.
2. **Arturo Ramos** — 27, overall 91. 23–1, 2.41 in 212.2 innings, Cy Young runner-up, three straight years of 32-plus starts and 200-plus innings. The most reliable volume in the group; he takes the ball every fifth day and keeps it in the park.
3. **Henry Rivas** — 30, overall 92, though I'd flag that he made only 22 starts and threw 136.1 innings in 2041 after back-to-back full seasons. Highest overall of the starters outside Coles, and a 2.64 ERA with 24 walks; the question with him is durability, not quality.
4. **John Ellis** — 26, overall 86. 20–3 over 189.2 innings, 3.42 ERA. He'll give you length — 86 stamina — and he's been a 32-start man two years running.
5. **Pablo Almanzar** — 23, overall 85 and trending up, but the record on him is thin: five starts, 34 innings in 2041. He's the fifth spot on paper, and I'd treat his workload as something to build rather than assume.

Behind them: **Mariano Rosales** closes — 42 saves, 1.84 ERA, overall 95. **Hitoki Ka** is the top setup arm — 0.90 ERA over 57 appearances in 2041.

Two caveats on the record. First, that's a depth chart from a five-man list; if Rivas's innings stay capped or Almanzar isn't stretched out, the fifth spot could move, and there's nobody at Las Vegas on my records to push for it. Second, where I have said "five" I'm reading it off the six starters on the roster — where the sixth, and any swing role, would slot in is a decision the field staff makes, not something my records settle. What I don't have is any stated plan from the manager or the pitching coach about usage or limits.

text:
Anthony — here's what my records show, and where they stop.

**The expiring money is where the conversation starts.** Four contracts run out after 2042, which means this winter is the last clean chance to get something back:

- **Darrin Davis, LF, 33** — $28.4M in 2042, free agent in 2043. Two MVPs, but 3.6 WAR last year at 33 with a big number. That's the most likely name moved.
- **Henry Rivas, SP, 30** — $28.2M in 2042, free agent in 2043. 3.2 WAR. A starter on an expiring deal is always askable.
- **Isley Kelley, SS, 34** — $25.0M in 2042, $25.0M in 2043, free agent in 2044. 7.4 WAR last season and still an MVP-caliber shortstop, but 34 with two years left and $50M on the books. The return would have to be real.
- **Hitoki Ka, RP, 30** — $7.0M in 2042, free agent in 2043. Cheap, effective bullpen arm — the kind of piece contenders call about.

**The second tier is the redundancy.** Kevin Clark (3B, 22, 0.048 service) and Giancarlo Hernandez (3B, 23, 0.003, out of options at 0/3) sit behind Quintero and Keane at third. Hernandez in particular can't be optioned, so he either makes the club or gets moved. Sidney Tumolo (2B, 26) is behind Taveras at second. Bobby Hendricks and Tommy Fry at Las Vegas are depth, not bait.

**Where I have to be straight with you:** "trade bait" is a judgment about what the front office intends, and I don't have that in my records. What I have is contracts, service time, options and roster status — which is what I just gave you. I'm not going to tell you a name is on the block when what I actually hold is an expiring deal and an inference.

And the counterweight to all of it: the budget shows $129.46M available with a $124.46M projected surplus. This club does not have to sell. Anyone moved this winter gets moved for talent, not for money.

One caution on the record itself: the service-time and option figures I read from are what's on file, and a couple of the lines in my roster carry oddities — Morton and Reyna show "last season 2042" with 0 WAR when 2042 hasn't been played, which reads to me as a data-entry artifact, not a scouting report. If you're printing a specific number off my sheet, let me confirm it against the source first.

q: How has the Oaks' season gone so far?
why: the question is about the oaks
text:
Anthony — here's the season as my records have it.

Thirteen games in, the Oaks are 11-2. They lost twice: in Indiana, 104-100, after being down 19 at the half and 20 after three, and at home to San Antonio, 126-117, in a Cup game with the score tied 90-90 going into the fourth. The five-game win streak ended with that Spurs loss. They're 3-1 in Cup play. Through 13 games they've won the fourth quarter ten times, lost it twice and tied it once. Current scoring is 113.9 a game, allowing 95.1.

The shape of the season: 0-4 in rookie camp and 0-5 in the preseason, 0-9 before a game that counted, then a 4-0 start that opened with the 85-82 home win over Charlotte — down 11 after three, won the fourth 36-22. Then the Indiana loss, then five straight wins over Toronto (135-75), Oklahoma City (101-95), Orlando (125-109), Philadelphia (120-106) and Denver in the Cup, a franchise-record 147-114 on 63 of 79 from the field, 80 percent, and 19 of 26 from three, with 40 assists and 5 turnovers. They were ranked number one in the NBA.com power rankings at 9-1, one of four ranked teams they had already beaten — Detroit at three, Oklahoma City at four, New York at six, Philadelphia at eight. Then San Antonio came in and won. This cycle they beat Denver at home 137-113 and won at Golden State 98-96 in a Cup game, coming back from 15 down at the half.

On the roster numbers: Adash Stanley 19.2 points, 6.2 assists, 53.8 percent from the field and 51.2 from three in 30.5 minutes. Austin Reaves 19.1 points in 32.9 minutes on 49.2 percent and 48.2 from three, and he's led or shared the team scoring lead in six of the thirteen games, including 32 against Denver in 22 minutes and 23 at Golden State. AJ Dybantsa 16.1 and 5.2 rebounds on 49.1 percent. Wendell Carter Jr. 10.4 and 9.6 on 64.1 percent. Dillon Brooks 12.5 in 28.1 minutes. Off the bench, Ty Jerome is at 15.2 points and 5.2 assists in 21.8 minutes on 59.1 percent, and has scored in double figures five straight games — 19, 28, 23, 14, 17. Harry Hayward, the second-round rookie on $4.5M, is at 7.6 and 5.2 in 17.5 minutes. Those are season to date.

What my records do not hold: I don't have a single-cycle injury list, I don't have minute restrictions, and I don't have anything on Jerami Grant's status beyond what the Tribune has printed — he failed his medical after the trade and the matter sits with the league, per Elias Varek in C112. B. Simmons has been a DNP six straight games and Coen Carr, James Jr. and Tate have sat with him, but whether that's a basketball decision or something else, the feed doesn't say and neither will I.

The one honest summary: the Oaks finish games. Trailed at the half in Detroit and Golden State and won both. Trailed after three in Philadelphia and Charlotte and won both. The two fourth quarters they lost were the one already decided in Orlando and the San Antonio game — and that's the only home loss on the record.
